It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.The Correlation EngineThe role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.The knowledge flywheelEach harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.The Knowledge FlywheelObserve collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.Putting the graph to workOn top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.If you want to build one of theseA fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.What comes nextThe graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.AcknowledgementsNone of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute
summary: By Dhruv PratapIntroductionOrganizations that have been around for a while usually run two identity systems side by side. One belongs to the cloud provider: IAM roles, instance profiles, execution roles. The other is your own, and it is the one your internal services actually check when they decide whether to answer a request.On infrastructure you build yourself, you can bootstrap your own identity however you like. On managed compute you cannot. The provider hands your process a cloud identity and nothing else.This post describes how we close that gap for Apache Spark workloads running on Amazon EMR. A workload that starts with only an AWS identity has to end up holding a first-class internal identity. Doing the exchange is straightforward. Making it trustworthy is the part that took the design work. Very little of what follows is specific to Spark or to EMR.Two identity systemsInternal service-to-service authentication at Netflix runs on a private PKI called Metatron. Every workload gets a short-lived X.509 certificate, and services authenticate each other with mutual TLS. A workload cannot simply ask for a certificate. It is issued only after the identity service has satisfied itself that the requester really is the workload it claims to be. That verification step is called attestation. In each environment we support (VMs, containers, functions) attestation rests on some environment-specific proof that the platform can check on its own.The second concept is the Data Project, which is our unit of ownership for data. A Data Project owns tables, has a set of authorized users, and has an identity of its own. Jobs run as the Data Project rather than as the person who launched them. That is what keeps table-level access control and audit consistent across scheduled and interactive use.So the problem is this. A Spark job on managed compute starts with an AWS execution role and no internal identity. Everything it needs from inside the company (reading an encrypted column, evaluating table ACLs, holding an interactive session open longer than a short-lived token lasts) requires the internal one.One identity, one roleThe design rests on a decision made outside the Spark stack entirely. Each Data Project identity maps 1:1 to a dedicated IAM role, and the service that owns Data Project metadata records that mapping.The mapping is what makes translation possible. It lets a statement in the provider’s vocabulary (“this process is running as role R”) become a statement in ours (“this process is workload W”). Without it there is nothing to translate into, and no amount of cryptography helps. The hard part of bridging two identity systems is rarely the protocol. It is committing to a mapping and then keeping it authoritative.One practical objection arrives immediately. A single AWS account cannot hold tens of thousands of IAM roles, and we expect data projects in the order of ten thousands. We handled this by sharding data project roles deterministically across a small pool of dedicated accounts, which scales well past the projected number of projects and has the useful side effect of keeping workload roles on the far side of an account boundary from the control planes that launch them.ComponentsFive components take part.The control plane is the only service allowed to launch Spark jobs. It resolves the Data Project’s IAM role, builds and signs a workload metadata payload, and submits the job with that role as the execution role. It holds a signing key issued to it for this purpose alone.The Data Project service is the authority for the identity-to-role mapping.The Identity service receives attestation requests, verifies them, and issues certificates.A Spark plugin provides the hook. Spark 3.0+ added a plugin interface with driver-side and executor-side components that are initialized while those processes are bootstrapping.AWS STS acts as a notary, which is not its usual job.Step one: the control plane makes a signed claimWhen a job is submitted, the control plane validates the caller, looks up the Data Project’s IAM role, and builds a small payload describing the workload it is about to launch. The payload names the application identity, the mapped role, and the environment, stack and detail that the resulting credentials should be scoped to. The control plane signs the payload and passes it and the signature through as ordinary job configuration.Two properties of this step matter. First, only one service can produce a valid signature, so the set of things that can assert “this workload is legitimate” is small and auditable. Second, the payload is a claim rather than an authority. On its own it proves nothing, because job configuration travels through infrastructure we do not fully control and anything that can read it can replay it.Step two: the workload proves it holds the cloud identityWhen the managed service launches the driver process, it does so under an OS user that has the execution role’s credentials available. The driver-side plugin initializes and uses those credentials to sign, but not send, a request to the provider’s identity endpoint (sts:GetCallerIdentity). The result is a short-lived pre-signed URL.That URL is a transferable proof of possession. Anyone can fetch it. Only the holder of the role’s credentials could have produced it. And the response comes from AWS rather than from the workload, stating which role signed the request. The workload cannot lie about the answer because the workload does not supply the answer.The pattern is not new. It is the same idea behind AWS IAM authentication in HashiCorp Vault and in AWS’s own function attestation flows. It generalizes well: any environment that gives a process cloud credentials and nothing else can still produce a verifiable statement about its own identity.The plugin sends one attestation request carrying both artifacts, the pre-signed URL and the signed metadata.Step three: corroborationThe identity service does four things.It fetches the pre-signed URL against AWS STS and reads back the role that signed it. This is the provider’s statement.It verifies the metadata signature against the key issued to the control plane. This is the platform’s statement.It corroborates the two. The role AWS reports must be the role the control plane said it dispatched, for the identity the metadata names.It issues certificates for that identity, scoped to the environment, stack and detail from the signed metadata.Step 3 is the point of the whole design. Neither statement is sufficient by itself, and they fail in complementary ways. The provider’s statement is unforgeable but under-specified: it gives you a role, and a role is not a workload. It says nothing about why this process exists or what it should be allowed to be. The platform’s statement is well-specified but unverifiable on its own, for the reasons above. Put together, the signature says the workload was legitimately dispatched and the pre-signed URL says this really is it. Neither party has to trust the workload’s own account of itself.There is a tension here that we settled deliberately, and other teams should expect to meet it. The provider’s answer identifies a role, not an application. Deriving an application name from a role name is fragile string matching, and the session identifiers the platform assigns are not under our control. We chose to take the application identity from the signed metadata and use the provider’s answer only for corroboration. That costs a network round trip and a stricter signing requirement, and it buys a much clearer trust story.The fan-out problemA Spark application is one driver and up to thousands of executors, created and destroyed throughout the life of a job. Attestation designed around one process per host does not survive that.There are two defensible answers.In the first, each executor attests independently. This is uniform, adds no new trust boundary, and grounds every process’s identity in the same provider-verified proof. The cost is amplification. One large job can produce thousands of STS calls and thousands of attestation requests in a burst, which looks a lot like an attack and creates a hard dependency on provider-side rate limits.In the second, executors inherit credentials from the driver. The driver attests once and distributes credentials to executors over Spark’s internal RPC, which we configure with authentication and AES-GCM encryption so that only processes in the same application can take part. Load on the identity service stays constant. The cost is a second trust boundary and a driver that is now a credential distribution point.Considering our scale at Netflix here we went with the second approach. The general lesson is that identity amplification is a capacity question, and it is better to answer it on purpose than to have it answered for you during an incident.LifecycleCertificates are short-lived by design, so bootstrapping is only half the work. On self-managed hosts a system service handles renewal. Inside managed compute there is no equivalent hook, so the driver JVM runs a timer that re-attests on a fixed interval, well ahead of expiry. Credential material is written to a temporary directory readable only by the process owner and removed when the process exits.Executors do not refresh. They are usually short-lived, and an executor that somehow outlives its credentials can exit and be replaced, which is cheaper than making every executor a renewal client.The rule worth carrying into any similar system is that attestation has to be a repeatable operation rather than a bootstrap step. Anything that can only happen once at process start will eventually be the reason a long-running job dies nine hours in.Why this generalizesIf you run your own identity system and are moving workloads onto managed compute, the specific services here matter less than the shape of the solution.Anchor on one exchangeable primitive. A single authoritative 1:1 mapping between your identity and a provider identity is what makes translation possible. The rest is plumbing.Require two independent claims and corroborate them. One from the provider, unforgeable and under-specified. One from your control plane, well-specified and replayable. Trust the intersection and never either alone.Keep the signer scarce. If exactly one service can make the platform’s claim, your trust story fits in a sentence.Hook the layer you still own. On managed compute you rarely control the host or its init system, but you almost always control the runtime: a plugin, an agent, an entrypoint. Attestation belongs there.Decide the amplification policy on purpose. Distributed engines multiply every per-process operation by their parallelism.Make attestation repeatable and credentials short-lived. Renewal is a requirement, not a follow-up.What makes the result trustworthy is that no single participant issues an identity by itself. Not the workload, not the control plane, not the provider. And the workload, which is the party in the weakest position to be trusted, is never asked to vouch for itself.AcknowledgementsThanks to Amer Hesson for the Data Project abstraction, Nick Siow for the Data Project IAM role sharding, and Doug Clark for Metatron attestation.Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
summary: By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen MareddyStratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1resources: numCpus: 8 memoryInMB: 18000 diskSizeInMB: 50000 networkInMbps: 1000Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.The Challenge: Over-ProvisioningWhen engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.Meet the Stratum Resource TunerTo address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:Figure 1: SRT Workflow High-LevelCollect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).Verify the recommendation through experiments.Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:Figure 2: Recommendation State MachineCREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.Metrics CollectionTo make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:Figure 3: Metrics CollectionExecution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:{ "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a", "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "tags.stratum.phase": "run", "tags.stratum.success": true, "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26, "tags.cpuCount": 8, "tags.memoryInMB": 18000, "tags.diskInMB": 50000, "tags.networkInMbps": 1000, "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1", "ts": 1780743028000}In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:{ "span_id": "38536313f65f060a", "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "phase": "run", "success": true, "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002, "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028, "runtime_secs": 26, "cpu_requested": 8, "memory_mb_requested": 18000, "disk_mb_requested": 50000, "network_mbps_requested": 1000, "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "env": "prod", "resource_usage": }Recommendation GenerationA scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.Figure 4: Recommendation Generation SequenceFor each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" } }, "experiment_inputs": null, "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null, "outcome_message": null, "finalized_at": null}As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.Retry with More ResourcesWe take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.Figure 5: Retry with More ResourcesThis “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.Recommendation VerificationEvery recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.Figure 6: Evaluating StageSynthetic experiment:Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.Typically runs for 1–2 hours.Runs to completion without early termination checks.Figure 7: Synthetic Experiment FlowProduction experiment:Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.Figure 8: Production Experiment FlowThe Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:{ "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7", "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 }, "productionExperiment": { "enabled": true, "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating }}Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:{ "outcome": "APPLIED", "syntheticExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }, "productionExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }}The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.Post-Apply MonitoringPassing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.Figure 9: Unexpected Retries SpikeBecause early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.Figure 10: Recommendation Auto-RevertWe intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.Where Are We TodayOversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 10% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.Looking ahead, our key priorities include:Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.CreditsSpecial thanks to Olof Johansson, Jakub Karczewski, Adam Mazur, Ethan Mathieu, Rosanna Lee, Ameya Vasani, Jean Barkhuysen, Paul Hieromnimon, and Adithya Prakash.Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Designing for sovereign AI: A shared foundation from edge to cloud
summary: As organizations apply AI to more business-critical and data-intensive workloads, AI processing is moving closer to where data is created, decisions are made, and operations take place. Manufacturers can analyze confidential production data next to the systems that generate it. Pharmaceutical companies can apply AI to clinical trials within controlled environments. Government agencies can run AI applications on sensitive information while maintaining established security and operational boundaries. This shift reflects ongoing innovation across the technology ecosystem to give organizations greater flexibility in where they run AI and process sensitive data, and it is changing the digital sovereignty conversation. It now encompasses where data is stored and processed, where workloads run, who can access and operate the systems around them, and how those systems remain secure and operational as requirements change. The next phase of digital sovereignty will take shape across the technology ecosystem, through closer alignment among silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI. Learn more about digital sovereignty As AI extends into more sensitive and mission-critical workloads, sovereignty must be designed across the stack, from silicon and infrastructure to cloud, data, and AI. Microsoft and Intel® are working together to help organizations create a more consistent foundation for innovation, while retaining greater choice over where workloads run and how they are controlled. A flexible sovereign architecture allows organizations to place each workload in the right environment, apply the controls it requires, and maintain a more consistent technology and operating foundation as requirements evolve. Sovereignty must work across the technology stack Sovereignty requirements vary by workload. The right level of control depends on factors such as data sensitivity, regulation, latency, connectivity, operational access, and resilience requirements. This creates a continuum, where organizations can apply different levels of control across public cloud, customer-controlled environments, and trusted partner solutions. Delivering that flexibility requires the underlying technology layers to work together. The controls that shape where a workload runs, how data is protected, who can access it, and how the environment is verified extend across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI. This is where the Microsoft and Intel partnership comes into focus. Together, we are working to create a more consistent foundation across these layers, giving organizations greater choice in where workloads run and how they are controlled. This principle is central to the work between Microsoft and Intel. Azure Local, running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors, brings distributed Azure infrastructure together with a common compute foundation for customer-controlled environments. Organizations can extend cloud and AI capabilities closer to their data and operations while maintaining consistent approaches to security, management, and governance. Trust must be designed for and verified For sensitive workloads, trust must be supported by technical protections and verifiable evidence. Organizations need to protect workloads across the technology stack and verify that systems are operating under the security conditions they have established. That starts at the compute layer and extends through identity, encryption, governance, policy, and operations. For supported Azure Confidential VM configurations, Intel® Xeon® processors provide hardware-based protections, including Intel® Trust Domain Extensions (Intel TDX), which can help isolate workloads while they are in use. Hardware-backed attestation can provide evidence that helps organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. Microsoft extends this foundation through security and governance controls across cloud and customer-controlled environments. Together, these capabilities can help organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. This is particularly important as AI brings regulated, proprietary, and mission-critical data into new workloads. Each workload should receive protections proportionate to its risk. Isolation, encryption, attestation, and operational controls can be applied where they provide meaningful value while preserving a manageable operating model across the broader environment. Digital sovereignty requires trust across the technology stack. Together, Intel and Microsoft are combining hardware-based security and confidential computing with cloud, AI and distributed infrastructure to help customers protect sensitive workloads and verify the environments in which they run. This shared foundation gives organizations greater control, confidence and choice, with the performance and scale to continue innovating as AI moves into more regulated and mission-critical environments. —Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security Sovereign AI brings intelligence closer to data Much of the data with the greatest potential for AI must remain within defined operational, regulatory, or security boundaries. This includes data tied to industrial operations, government services, clinical environments, intellectual property, and proprietary research. Workload placement has therefore become a practical AI decision. Organizations need the flexibility to run AI closer to their data, applications, and operations. Delivering that flexibility requires infrastructure, cloud platforms, AI software, and security capabilities to work as a connected foundation. Microsoft Foundry helps organizations build and deploy AI applications and models, with options for where AI runs based on their requirements. Foundry Local enables organizations to run AI inference in their own environments, closer to the data and applications those models rely on. On the same infrastructure, Intel Xeon 6 processors with Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX) can accelerate AI workloads directly on the CPU. Intel® OpenVINO™ helps developers optimize and deploy models across supported infrastructure. This approach extends across the broader application environment. Organizations may need to manage AI, applications, data, development, and productivity workloads within the same governance and operational boundary. Microsoft 365 Local and GitHub Enterprise Local extend customer-controlled options to collaboration, source code, and software development workflows. Sovereign AI brings models, data, applications, development tools, and infrastructure together under the controls each workload requires. This approach allows organizations to apply AI within the operational and governance boundaries established for their most sensitive data. Organizations want to apply AI to their most valuable data while maintaining the controls that data requires. On supported Azure confidential VM configurations, Intel TDX helps make that possible by running AI workloads in hardware-isolated trust domains, protecting models and data while in use and isolating them from the host and hypervisor. Hardware-backed attestation then gives organizations evidence they can check against their own requirements, so they can move from trusting their environment to verifying it. —Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security Sovereignty architecture must be adaptable Sovereignty requirements will continue to change. A workload that runs in a connected environment today may face different regulatory, resilience, or connectivity requirements tomorrow. AI models, applications, and infrastructure will also continue to evolve. A sovereign architecture must therefore provide control without creating rigidity. Organizations should be able to adapt where workloads run, how they are secured, and how they connect without rebuilding their management and security model each time requirements change. This is another reason partnership across the technology stack matters. Alignment across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI software can give organizations a more stable foundation even as individual technologies and workload requirements evolve. A well-designed sovereign architecture gives organizations room to respond as regulations, technologies, and operating conditions change. Explore Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe Discover how Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe helps organizations address evolving data sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements while accelerating cloud and AI innovation. Learn more Three questions leaders should ask Digital sovereignty can become abstract quickly. A better place to start is the workload. 1. What must remain under your control? Consider the data, infrastructure, administrative access, software operations, and connectivity on which the workload depends. The answer may differ by application, even within the same organization. 2. Can you verify that those controls are working? Policies and contractual commitments are important, but sensitive workloads may also require technical evidence. Consider how your architecture supports encryption, isolation, identity and access control, policy enforcement, attestation, and operational transparency. 3. Will the architecture leave you room to adapt? AI capabilities, regulations, operating conditions, and workload requirements will continue to change. Your architecture should allow you to adopt new models, move processing closer to data, and adjust where workloads run without creating an entirely separate technology environment each time. Digital sovereignty depends on cloud, infrastructure, security, AI, and silicon working together. Our collaboration with Intel gives customers a more consistent foundation across these layers, so they can apply stronger controls where needed while retaining the flexibility to innovate. —Bernardo Caldas, CVP, Azure Edge Product Management The strongest sovereignty strategy preserves choice Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control over the technology and data they depend on while preserving their capacity to innovate. Achieving that outcome requires collaboration across the technology ecosystem. Microsoft and Intel are connecting silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI to give organizations greater flexibility in where workloads run, how they are protected, and how they evolve. A shared foundation across these layers allows organizations to apply the right controls to each workload and benefit from advances across the broader technology ecosystem. A strong sovereignty strategy meets today’s requirements while preserving tomorrow’s options. Resources to learn more Dive deeper into digital sovereignty to learn how Microsoft is helping organizations address data residency, operational control, security, and regulatory requirements across cloud and customer-controlled environments. Learn more about Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud. Join us at Microsoft Ignite in November to hear the latest on Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, Azure Local, AI, security, and infrastructure innovation. title: [Engineering at Meta] The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
summary: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. The Problem: More Context, Worse Results Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers We split the system into two layers: A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router. Fourteen specialized subagents, each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug. The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates). Gather required fields from the user. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations). Reliability gate check for active warnings or required reviewers. Delegate to the subagent with full context. Handle results and surface errors, confirm success. Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded. What We Built: Workflow Templates, Not New Agents One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space: Column Onboarding: Schema → Validation → Population → Testing Event Onboarding: Schema → Population → Validation → Testing → Event Processing Pipeline Migration: Assessment → Planning → Population → Validation → Monitoring Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability. Each subagent follows a standardized structure: Knowledge sources: which domain files to load at runtime (typically a few thousand tokens each). Pre-gathering checklist: what the orchestrator must collect before delegation. Step-by-step workflow: the domain-specific execution plan. Discovery patterns: how to find relevant code patterns in the monorepo. Troubleshooting: error-to-resolution mappings for common failures. This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first. Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain. When a knowledge file is updated, the next session automatically uses the latest version — no orchestrator changes required. The same knowledge files serve multiple platform implementations of our agent. Results Configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with our earlier config-driven system. The thin orchestrator system does it in under an hour. For broader context: About two-thirds of the system’s changes land without significant human edits. It gets there by trading generality for deep domain knowledge, a deliberate architectural choice. The orchestrator is general; the subagents are specialists. Why This Works (And Why Heavyweight Orchestrators Don’t) The conventional approach is to make the orchestrator the smartest component — give it all the context and let it reason about what to do and how to do it. This works until it doesn’t, and it stops working exactly when you need it most — at scale, with complex multi-step workflows, across heterogeneous subsystems. The thin orchestrator works because it aligns architectural boundaries with computational boundaries: Deterministic decisions stay deterministic. “Which subagent handles this?” is a routing decision, not a reasoning task. Don’t use an LLM for it. Context isolation prevents cross-contamination. The population agent for data source A never sees data source B’s patterns. It can’t hallucinate the wrong one. Failures are contained. If a subagent fails, the orchestrator retries or escalates. The failure doesn’t corrupt the orchestrator’s state or other subagents’ contexts. The system improves at every layer independently. A better model improves all 14 subagents simultaneously. A knowledge file update takes effect immediately. A new workflow template unlocks new capabilities without touching agents. No single component carries the full weight. How to Apply This to Your AI Agents This pattern isn’t specific to data pipelines. Any team building production AI agents can benefit: Separate routing from reasoning. If your orchestrator is making domain decisions, it’s doing too much. Routing should be deterministic: keyword matching, intent classification, field gathering. Push all domain reasoning into isolated subagents. Design subagents as structurally uniform specialists. Every subagent should have the same structure: knowledge sources, required inputs, execution steps, error handling. This makes adding new capabilities templated work rather than architecture changes. Use workflow templates, not new agents, to scale. When you need a new use case, first ask: Can I sequence existing agents differently? If you can’t reuse agents across workflows, your agents are too coupled to specific use cases. Load knowledge at runtime, not at build time. Embed knowledge in the orchestrator and every update requires redeployment. Load it on demand and updates take effect immediately, across all platforms. Draw the deterministic/probabilistic boundary explicitly. For every component, decide: Is this a routing decision (deterministic) or a reasoning task (probabilistic)? The orchestrator should be on one side, the subagents on the other. Don’t mix them. The strongest argument for a thin orchestrator is the failure mode of the alternative. When a heavyweight orchestrator hallucinates, the error spreads to everything downstream: it routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields, or skips reliability checks. A thin orchestrator leaves little room for hallucination because its routing and reliability steps don’t rely on LLM reasoning. It follows a fixed protocol. The creativity happens downstream, in isolated, domain-scoped contexts where hallucination risk is minimized and failures are contained. What’s Next We’re scaling this architecture to handle an increase in data columns across new pipeline domains. The compositional thesis predicts this will work because scaling means adding workflow templates and knowledge files, not rebuilding agents. We’re also exploring how the system can continuously improve from production usage, using automated feedback loops to identify failure patterns and propose targeted improvements to subagent knowledge, with human review always gating any changes. The counterintuitive lesson: the most important component in our AI agent system is the one that does the least work. Keep your orchestrator thin and your specialists deep, and the whole system becomes more reliable. Acknowledgements This work was a team effort. Some other people who contributed to this effort include: Mani Bhushan, Rahul Maliakkal, Jae Ha, Chakrapani Kumar, Vivek Tiwari, and Amanda Yin. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: Prime Day 2026 by the numbers, Claude Haiku 5.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, and more (October 13, 2026)
summary: Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong. The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used. The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Claude Haiku 5.5 is now available on AWS – You can now use the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS, at around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It’s the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence per task instead of fixing one setting for a whole workload. It pairs naturally with Claude Opus 5.5: Opus plans and makes the judgment calls, and because Haiku is fast and cheap, you can run many Haiku subagents in parallel for routing, classification, and small code changes across many files. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic for voice agents – You can now build real-time voice agents on a speech-to-speech Amazon Nova model with better reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, plus lower latency. That combination matters for multi-step work: a support agent can look up an order, check return eligibility, and start the return inside one conversation. It keeps expressive voices in seven languages, controllable turn-taking, and a 256K context window, and pairs with Strands Bidi Agents, now generally available, to get a production voice agent going in a few lines of code. Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection now detects data exfiltration and destruction – Amazon GuardDuty now looks past login anomalies to the queries themselves on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. RDS Protection for data activity builds behavioral baselines and uses ML-based anomaly detection plus threat intelligence to flag unusual data access, with no agents, extra infrastructure, or database configuration changes. This closes a real gap: once an attacker has valid credentials from phishing or a misconfiguration, their queries can look indistinguishable from your application’s. AWS Lambda supports OAuth for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources – You can now authenticate Lambda Kafka consumers through your enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta. Event source mappings previously supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mTLS, which left teams in regulated industries unable to use Kafka ESM at all. Now you get the automatic scaling, batching, error handling, and event filtering of Kafka ESM with the same identity governance you apply everywhere else. It works with self-hosted clusters and managed offerings including Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. Amazon Redshift adds Apache Iceberg materialized views – You can now pre-compute expensive joins and aggregations once in Amazon Redshift and store the result as an Iceberg table in Amazon S3, registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. You create them with familiar SQL, and the results are immediately queryable by any Iceberg-compatible engine, including Amazon Athena, Apache Spark, Trino, and Snowflake. Redshift keeps them current by recomputing only what changed. There’s a good deep dive on the AWS Big Data blog if you want the details. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Introducing Strands Box: AI agent sandboxes powered by Dogwood – As more of us let agents run shell commands and call APIs without approving every step, isolation alone stops being enough. Strands Box is an open source sandbox (Apache 2.0, developer preview) that combines OS-level containment with fine-grained policies written in Dogwood, so permissions can depend on what the agent has already done. You can say “let the agent post to the incident channel, but no more than three times every 10 minutes” and have that enforced from outside the agent’s process. It also keeps real credentials out of the agent’s environment by attaching them at an egress gateway. AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security – Related to that theme, AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now integrates into your CI/CD pipeline in public preview, turning penetration testing into a deploy-time event instead of something that happens off to the side. Developers get findings with severity, affected endpoints, and remediation guidance right in the pipeline output, and the pipeline re-tests to verify fixes. How Postman runs Agent Mode for 40 million developers on Amazon Bedrock – A look at the architecture behind a feature serving a very large developer audience. Worth reading if you’re moving an agentic feature from a demo to something that has to hold up under real traffic. ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026 – If you lost track of a month that included a lot of model launches, this is a tidy catch-up in one place. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, and reserved seating is now open. The session catalog is live, so register and claim your spots in chalk talks, workshops, and builders’ sessions before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, and this is a busy stretch. Upcoming stops include San Francisco (October 13), Miami (October 14), Brisbane (October 16), Cape Town (October 16), Malta (October 16), and Mumbai (October 17). Here in Brazil, the community calendar has more editions coming before the end of the year. title: [HashiCorp] Secure AI agents with HashiCorp Boundary
summary: Locally running cowork and coding AI agents are evolving from passive assistants into active participants in enterprise IT operations -analyzing logs, investigating incidents, assessing system health, and recommending next steps. While this can accelerate troubleshooting and reduce operational toil, enterprise adoption requires answering a critical question beyond improving productivity: How can an AI agent interact with infrastructure without creating new security, compliance, or governance risks? This blog explores how to leverage HashiCorp Boundary’s zero trust access model to provide AI agents with secure, governed access to infrastructure resources. To explore this challenge in practice, we used IBM technologies and services to create an AI agent that runs on developer workstation and is capable of investigating infrastructure incidents through natural-language requests. For example, a platform engineer can ask the agent to analyze a performance issue, gather diagnostic data from a target system, and summarize the findings. The key objective was not only to build an AI agent but to ensure that every infrastructure interaction remained secure, controlled, and auditable. The solution overview The AI agent enables a platform engineer to describe an operational goal in natural language: A sample prompt can be: “Investigate memory pressure on app-server-01 and summarize the findings.” The following diagram shows the architecture and workflow for an AI agent built with IBM Bob. The AI agent uses watsonx and Granite models to interpret an operational request, develop an investigation plan, execute the required diagnostic actions, analyze the results, and produce a concise summary for the platform engineer. When infrastructure access is required, the AI agent running on the platform engineer workstation initiates a login to Boundary, and the platform engineer completes the authentication on behalf of the agent. The AI agent then opens a Boundary-proxied session to the authorized Linux target to perform the investigation. Session activity is recorded, and audit logs capture authentication events, access decisions, grants, policy changes, and administrative actions. This creates a human-authorized workflow for an AI-assisted operation without relying on fully unattended infrastructure access. The zero trust layer As shown in the architecture diagram, Boundary provides the secure access layer between the AI agent and the target infrastructure. Rather than granting the agent direct access to systems, Boundary evaluates the authenticated user's identity, permissions, and target access policies before establishing a connection. This separation of access control from AI reasoning ensures that infrastructure access remains governed by enterprise security policies. Secure access with Boundary In this model, Boundary enables five essential controls: Identity-based authentication: Boundary delegates authentication to IBM Verify through an OIDC authentication method and applies access policies to the verified identity. Zero trust connectivity: The agent reaches the target only through an active Boundary session, without requiring the agent host to have a direct network route or VPN access to the target’s private network. Boundary workers proxy the connection to the target. Target grants: Least-privilege grants restrict network access to only the Linux targets required for the agent’s operational task. Secrets management: Vault stores or generates target credentials, including short-lived dynamic credentials. Boundary retrieves and injects the credentials when it establishes the session, without returning them to the agent or platform engineer. This ensures credentials are shared, leaked, stolen, or insecurely stored. Administrative control: Authorized administrators can cancel an active session, providing a kill switch for infrastructure access. Auditability and session recording Boundary captures the agent’s infrastructure activity within the same governed access layer used for human operators. Session recordings provide visibility into session interactions and the associated target, user, host, and connection metadata. Boundary also emits audit events for authenticated requests, session activity, and administrative operations. Together, session recording and audit events provide centralized evidence for incident reviews, security investigations, and compliance validation, helping organizations treat the AI agent as a controlled and auditable participant in enterprise operations. Demo The video demonstrates how an AI agent uses a Platform Engineer’s verified identity and permissions to access enterprise resources through Boundary with governance and auditability. Final thoughts As AI agents move from analysis to infrastructure action, enterprises must embed security, governance, and accountability directly into the workflow. Automation alone is not enough; organizations also need controls that govern identity, access, credentials, sessions, and evidence. In this example, we used watsonx.ai to support the agent’s reasoning, planning, and summarization; Boundary to authorize and proxy infrastructure access; Verify to authenticate the platform engineer; and Vault to manage and inject target credentials. Together, these technologies create a secure, governed model for agent-assisted enterprise operations. The agent can help perform infrastructure tasks while operating within the identity, access, session, and audit controls expected from human operators. Building the AI agent You can try testing this workflow out in your environment. There are several possible approaches, but you can build your AI agent and enable secure access to your resources using Boundary by setting up the services and accounts as described below: IBM Cloud and watsonx.ai: Create an IBM Cloud account and use watsonx.ai python SDK to build the agent. IBM watsonx.ai provides access to the foundation models and tools that an AI agent can use for reasoning, planning, and summarization. You can also use IBM Bob, an agentic development partner, to design and implement the AI agent through natural-language prompts. Alternatively, you can use the AI agentic frameworks of your choice to develop your AI agent. Linux host or cloud VM: Create a Linux host in your cloud environment or infrastructure for the agent to inspect. IBM Verify: Sign-up for an Identity Provider (IdP) like IBM Verify. Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) and create a user account. A platform engineer will use this account to authenticate Boundary before the agent opens a session. You can also use other IdPs of your choice. HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP) account: Create a free HCP account, deploy Boundary and Vault clusters and complete the following configurations: Configure the Linux host as a Boundary target. Enable session recording for the target and configure an Amazon S3 or supported S3-compatible storage bucket and the applicable storage policies. Store the host credentials in a Boundary static credential store, or, preferably, configure a Vault credential library. Bind the credential source to the SSH target as an injected application credential. Credential injection removes the need for the agent to receive the target credential. Configure Verify as an OIDC authentication provider in Boundary and set the OIDC method as the primary method. Configure Boundary roles and grants to give the authenticated identity least-privilege access to the required target. Local development environment: Install Python and the Boundary CLI on your development machine. The AI agent developed calls watsonx.ai python APIs and connects to the target through a Boundary-proxied session after the platform engineer authenticates.
