title: [Kubernetes] Spotlight on SIG Apps
summary: As Kubernetes adoption has grown, the conversation has shifted beyond running containers to managing increasingly complex application lifecycles. Modern platforms support stateless web services, stateful databases, batch processing, AI workloads, and platform services. At the same time, they must remain reliable during upgrades, scaling events, and infrastructure failures. Every Kubernetes user relies on SIG Apps, whether they realize it or not. Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs form the foundation of how applications are deployed, updated, scaled, and operated across the Kubernetes ecosystem. SIG Apps is focused on improving workload resilience, refining application lifecycle management, and addressing the operational challenges that emerge when applications encounter node failures, rollout disruptions, and increasingly complex infrastructure environments. In this spotlight, we sit down with two of the three SIG Apps chairs Janet Kuo and Maciej Szulik to discuss the evolution of Kubernetes workload management, the challenges of balancing application reliability with operational simplicity, and the future of application lifecycle management within one of Kubernetes’ most influential Special Interest Groups. Introducing SIG AppsNatalie Fisher: Can you introduce yourself, your role, and how you got involved in SIG Apps? Janet Kuo: I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. In those early days, my focus was on building the core Workloads API, specifically developing controllers like Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, and DaemonSet, defining their rollout behaviors, and bringing them from initial designs to GA. That hands-on work was my entry point into SIG Apps. Since then, I've stayed deeply involved in both the technical and community sides of Kubernetes. I have led SIG Apps as Co-Chair and Tech Lead since 2019. Currently, in addition to maintaining the workloads API, I am driving new subprojects like the Agent Sandbox to ensure Kubernetes is ready for next-generation agentic and AI workloads. Maciej Szulik: I started contributing to Kubernetes all the way back in 2014. Since then, I've worked across various areas of the project: controllers, kubectl, and apimachinery, which eventually led me to become one of the Chairs and Tech Leads for SIG Apps. My current focus is reliability of the workload controllers under the SIG Apps umbrella and stability and ease of use of kubectl as part of my SIG CLI Tech Lead role. I also care about overall community health and growth as part of my Steering Committee role. Outside of Kubernetes, I work as a Staff Platform Engineer at Defense Unicorns, where I'm helping make Kubernetes more airgap-native with a project called zarf. The problem and the solutionSIG Apps is responsible for the core workload APIs that power how applications run on Kubernetes. From Deployments and StatefulSets to Jobs and CronJobs, these controllers determine how workloads are created, updated, scaled, and recovered when things go wrong. As Kubernetes expands to support increasingly diverse workloads – including AI, batch processing, and large-scale distributed applications – SIG Apps continues to evolve these APIs while balancing reliability, backward compatibility, and operational simplicity. NF: For readers who may not be familiar, what is SIG Apps, and what role does it play within the broader Kubernetes ecosystem? MS: SIG Apps is the Kubernetes Special Interest Group responsible for the workloads APIs. CronJob and Job help running batch workloads, whereas DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, and StatefulSet serve the majority of other applications. More broadly, SIG Apps owns the layer most developers actually touch day-to-day: the controllers that turn a workload specification into running, self-healing pods. It's the group deciding how Deployments roll out, how Jobs retry, how DaemonSets place a pod per node. JK: Adding to what Maciej described, as the industry shifts, we are seeing a massive demand to run complex, non-traditional workloads like distributed AI training, batch computing, and dynamic agent environments. Our role is expanding: we aren't just maintaining the classic workloads API, but we are actively evolving it and establishing new patterns (like the Agent Sandbox) to make sure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI. NF: Looking at the workload APIs owned by SIG Apps (Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs), which areas are receiving the most attention from maintainers and contributors? MS: After a long stretch focused on making batch workloads run smoothly on Kubernetes, we’ve shifted attention to make sure serving workloads (DaemonSets, StatefulSets, etc) aren’t left behind. This means performance and high-scale improvements to rollout and scaling behavior, plus working through our backlog of user-reported issues, prioritizing the ones with the strongest support from the user base. Current focus areasAs Kubernetes workloads grow in scale and complexity, the challenges facing workload controllers evolve as well. We asked the SIG Apps chairs where contributors are focusing their efforts today and which resilience problems they believe are the highest priorities. NF: From your perspective, what are the most important workload resilience problems SIG Apps is trying to solve today? MS: Node lifecycle challenges have come up repeatedly across SIG Apps, SIG Node, and SIG Autoscaling discussions. DaemonSets and Jobs are just where the pain is most visible, since they're the workloads most directly bound to node state. Rather than solve it piecemeal within one SIG, we've settled on spinning up a dedicated Node Lifecycle Working Group to focus on this properly and hopefully land long-term solutions instead of one-off patches. JK: From an AI perspective, resilience is critical. When you are running a massive distributed LLM training job that spans hundreds of GPUs, a single node failure can halt the entire pipeline. Similarly, if a DaemonSet that runs your logging or GPU monitoring agent gets stuck on a bad node, it impacts the entire cluster's health. In addition to the work in the Node Lifecycle WG to handle infrastructure-level degradation, SIG Apps is addressing this at the orchestration layer through subprojects like JobSet (for distributed training) and LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) (for sharded LLM inference). These APIs introduce patterns like "all-or-nothing" failure handling, where a single pod or job failure triggers a coordinated group-level restart to resume from the last clean checkpoint, rather than letting stuck workloads hang in an inconsistent state. Real-world impactThe work happening within SIG Apps extends far beyond controller implementations and API design. We wanted to understand what these improvements mean in practice for platform teams operating Kubernetes clusters in production. NF: For platform teams operating Kubernetes in production, what practical improvements would they notice if the node lifecycle and workload resilience work currently under discussion is successfully delivered? MS: I’m mostly looking from the sidelines, the folks actually in the Node Lifecycle Working Group would give you a sharper answer. But from where I sit, I’m hoping their work translates into fewer 3am pages that turn out to be “a DaemonSet rollout got stuck because node X was flaky, and someone had to manually cordon/delete/restart to unstick it.” JK: +1 to what Maciej said, and beyond reducing manual intervention, platform teams will also see much better resource predictability and cost efficiency. For example, in AI workloads where GPU idle time is extremely expensive, having Kubernetes automatically detect a degraded node and reschedule the training coordinator or agent before the job crashes means less wasted compute and more stable job execution. Challenges and trade-offsEvolving APIs that millions of workloads rely on requires careful engineering and even more careful decision-making. We asked the SIG Apps chairs about the technical and operational trade-offs they weigh when introducing changes to Kubernetes’ core workload controllers. NF: What are some of the hardest technical or operational trade-offs SIG Apps encounters when evolving core workload controllers? MS: Honestly, a few tensions keep coming up: how aggressively a controller should give up on stuck pods, and what signals it actually needs to make that call correctly. At the same time, we always have to think about backward compatibility. Deployment, DaemonSet, and Job behavior has been depended on for a decade , so even a change that’s clearly “more correct” can break automation people built around the old behavior without meaning to. JK: One of our hardest trade-offs is resisting the urge to make "elegant" design changes that break backward compatibility. Instead, we have to design opt-in features that let users adopt new behaviors without forcing them on legacy workloads. When we need to support completely new paradigms, we prefer introducing them as CRDs first rather than bloating the core APIs, like we are doing with Agent Sandbox, JobSet, and LWS. Looking aheadWhile much of SIG Apps’ work focuses on maintaining the stability of existing workload APIs, the group is also shaping the future of Kubernetes through new enhancements and proposals. We concluded by asking about one proposal that recently returned to active development and what it represents for the future of workload management. NF: The SIG recently discussed reviving KEP-4443 with a target release of Kubernetes 1.38. What opportunities or challenges does this proposal aim to address, and why is now the right time to revisit it? KEP-4443 addresses a small but real gap in the Job API: a PodFailurePolicy can be configured to add a condition reason to the JobFailed condition, but different pod failure policy rules targeting different container exit codes all produce that same generic reason. The proposal is simple: an optional Name field on each PodFailurePolicyRule, which gets appended to the JobFailed condition reason, so higher-level tools like JobSet can finally react differently depending on which rule triggered the failure. As for timing, the answer is as simple as it always is in open source: we lost the original contributor who was driving this. Now we’ve got someone new interested in picking it up, that’s why we’re targeting the next release. Getting InvolvedNF: For someone interested in contributing to SIG Apps, where would you recommend they start, especially if they are not yet a Kubernetes maintainer? MS: The best place to start is the #sig-apps slack channel and our regular SIG Apps meetings. We’ve all started there, and if it feels intimidating, or nobody replies right away, that’s completely normal. Everyone's busy. It's not personal. JK: In addition to what Maciej answered, I'd suggest looking at our newer subprojects and initiatives. Contributing to stable APIs like Deployment or StatefulSet can be daunting because the barrier for making changes is very high due to backward compatibility, and there is much less low-hanging fruit. If you are new to the community, projects like the Agent Sandbox are fantastic entry points. They are actively evolving, have a friendly group of maintainers, and offer plenty of greenfield development opportunities where you can make a significant impact quickly. SummarySIG Apps has shaped how Kubernetes applications are deployed and operated since the project’s earliest days. While users often interact with Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, and DaemonSets without thinking about the controllers behind them, the work within SIG Apps continues to shape the reliability and scalability of workloads across the Kubernetes ecosystem. From improving workload resilience and node lifecycle behavior to enabling new patterns for AI and distributed computing, the SIG is evolving Kubernetes while remaining committed to one of the project’s core principles: preserving the stability and backward compatibility that users depend on. Whether you’re interested in core workload APIs, emerging projects like Agent Sandbox, or helping improve the operational experience of Kubernetes users everywhere, SIG Apps offers many opportunities to get involved.

title: [CNCF] Deploying, maintaining, and migrating production n8n on EKS
summary: n8n is easy to try and harder to run under production traffic. A single container with SQLite works great for a quick demo. Production is a different story entirely. You need workers, webhook processors, PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage, external secrets, ingress routing, and an upgrade plan that preserves workflow history. Engineering teams rely on n8n to connect internal systems, process webhooks, and automate critical business data pipelines. It is also showing up in AI workloads, including self-hosted agents and RAG pipelines. Those workloads can put more pressure on workers, secrets management, and state handling.We deployed n8n on Amazon EKS, ran it under real traffic, and later moved from a community Helm chart to n8n’s official Helm chart. The platform stayed in place, and we kept the database, queue, object storage, IAM role, and secrets intact through the cutover. Why we started with the community chart The community chart got us to production. It supported queue mode, additional ingress configuration, and StatefulSet-based main pods, which matched our architectural requirements at the time. We ran it for about a year. Over time, maintaining unsupported features and local patches became harder to justify. We compared the available options and decided to move to the official chart, where ongoing maintenance and active community support gave us a clearer path for future upgrades. How we ran n8n We ran n8n in queue mode on EKS. In queue mode, the main instance manages workflow information and triggers, while worker instances execute jobs from the Redis queue. Dedicated webhook processors handled production webhook traffic separately. We split ingress by traffic type. Public webhooks ran behind an internet-facing load balancer, while internal webhooks used a private hostname. That separation fit our traffic patterns. Workers handled workflow execution. PostgreSQL stored workflow and execution data, Redis handled queued jobs, and S3 stored binary files. Because licensing multi-replica main pods is an Enterprise capability, we needed a secure, consistent way to handle shared application configuration and encryption key secrets across pods. We stored those secrets in AWS Secrets Manager and synced them into Kubernetes using External Secrets Operator (ESO). This synchronized application credentials, API keys, and environment variables into Kubernetes Secrets. What changed with the official chart The community chart ran the main pod as a StatefulSet with one persistent volume per replica. Workers and webhook processors already ran as Deployments. That StatefulSet configuration avoided multi-attach issues on AWS gp3 ReadWriteOnce (RWO) EBS volumes when running more than one main pod. In our configuration, the official chart used a different workload model, with main running as a Deployment and persistence relying on a single shared PVC. Our gp3 volume could not attach to multiple main pods across nodes, so an in-place Helm upgrade did not fit the deployment. We treated the migration as a full cutover instead. The shared persistence requirement was our main design decision. We checked what was stored on disk before carrying it forward: PostgreSQL held workflow and execution data. Redis held queued jobs. S3 held files. AWS Secrets Manager held the encryption key and application secrets. We found nothing on the main pod volume that needed to persist. With PostgreSQL, Redis, S3, and Secrets Manager holding the required application state, a replacement main pod could start and reconnect without relying on a pod-specific disk. We disabled main persistence entirely for the official chart deployment. Moving traffic safely The platform stayed in place: we kept the database, object storage, IAM role, and secrets through the cutover. Everything else was recreated from the new chart values. Before the production migration, we: Tested rollback in a non-prod environment Took a database snapshot Saved secrets to a secondary location Did not change the n8n image version. A version bump could trigger a database migration, and we wanted to keep the database out of the cutover story We tested in non-production first with a restored database snapshot: pods healthy, known workflows completing, required endpoints reachable. We verified rollback there before touching live traffic. The Helm release changed. PostgreSQL, Redis, S3, IAM, and secrets stayed. For a public example of how we structure official-chart values for external Postgres/Redis, queue mode + HPA, resources, ingress/webhooks, optional task runners, see: github.com/husne-fairwinds/n8n-sample Fairwinds helps teams manage Kubernetes environments, with a focus on operational reliability, security, and maintainability.

title: [Cloudflare] Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust
summary: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain.Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like.Performance and memory improvementsEarly benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers:As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs, and we’re hoping to find more.You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration.By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster:Try tsrsTypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm:npm install tsrs npx tsrsWhy now?We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go.However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript.Why Rust?You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?”However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency.Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before.This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application.How will the tsrs port be maintained?First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post:Each morning, an agent reviews the changes, fetches diffs, and opens tracking issues for anything that could affect Vinext. Every night, the compatibility matrix is regenerated as we run the Next.js test suite against Vinext. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix.We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins.Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release.What’s next?Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc. We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

title: [Cloudflare] Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
summary: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April, an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave.Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before.About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in.How a review doubled in costThe chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data.The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though.At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models.Our internal standards reviewer, Codex, ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself.The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost.What else has changed since our last post?One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out!So, where were the tokens going?Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again.That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both.It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it.That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls.Sharing a cached prefix between every repositoryBeginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider.The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits.The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written.On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs.The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72.Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release.Fewer calls, fewer dollarsThe next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review.ChangeWhat was happeningEffect of changeRemoving tools that reviewers couldn't useSub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering.One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer requestReading files in parallelIn 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file.Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KBSkipping reviewers on re-reviewsAbout two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at.On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%.Stopping after the review is postedOpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw.About $0.07 saved per jobTreating a slow reviewer differently from a broken providerA reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit.Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost noneCanceling canceled jobsGitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished.Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelledThe most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it.A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer.Changing models and effortThe next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked.When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving.Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment.The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings.Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%.The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5.On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below.To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that.LatencyWe weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers.The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30.By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been.Review qualityA cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened.With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions.First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence.Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews.Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low.Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical.So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next.Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems.Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%.Where this leaves usAn average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each session’s first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside.Lower cost reviews didn’t automatically mean worse quality, but it didn’t automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level you’re paying for.If you’re at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, I’m talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, It’s time to build, not buy, on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. I’ll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.

title: [Cloudflare] Continuous accountability for Verified bots
summary: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug.As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria:Identify yourself accurately and securelyDo only what you say you will doDon’t engage in abusive behaviorBots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm.Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.”This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important:Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next.Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior.For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked.Do not engage in abusive behaviorThis simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are:Does the bot respect instructions?Did it respond to direct feedback?We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar, as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify.When in Rome, do as the Romans doA robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time.Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309.And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals.What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on othersBots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again.Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it.Building trust over timeObserving these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them.This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management, forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone.We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior.Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar.And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

title: [Dropbox Tech] Evolving our calendar assistant Reclaim to be AI-native without starting over
summary: Calendars hold more than just blocks of time. They reflect how people plan their days, coordinate with others, and make room for what matters to them. Reclaim, the Dropbox-owned calendar assistant, helps manage that complexity by using AI to find and adjust time for tasks, habits, and meetings. That approach works well when inputs and expected outcomes are clear. But people also use Reclaim for scheduling that’s less straightforward. As AI assistants and natural-language interfaces became more capable, they opened up a new way for people to use Reclaim. We imagined situations where users could describe a scheduling goal in their own words, even when it didn’t map neatly to an existing setting or command. Words alone wouldn’t be enough to determine what should happen on a real calendar, though. Reclaim still needs the context that gives requests meaning, including what’s already scheduled, when a user is available, and which preferences and commitments impact changes. Connecting natural-language requests with the surrounding calendar context could help people spend less time figuring out which settings or actions to use. But building the experience required more than adding an AI interface to the existing product. We needed to rethink how Reclaim turned conversational requests into calendar changes while preserving the scheduling system already in place. Evolving Reclaim for AI without starting over For our engineers, the rebuild started with the way Reclaim already managed calendars. Calendar changes carry real weight because time is precious and scheduled events often involve other people. Any new AI capability needed to feel like a natural extension of Reclaim, and it needed to work with the scheduling logic already in place. Before the redesign, Reclaim handled calendar changes in two primary ways. Users could make specific changes themselves, like moving an event or updating a setting. And Reclaim’s automated scheduler also worked in the background. It considered each person’s preferences and availability when finding time for tasks, focus work, and recurring routines like lunch, then adjusted those calendar blocks as schedules changed. The emergence of AI agents introduced a potential third way for users to use Reclaim. Instead of choosing a specific setting or command, a user might prefer to describe what they want to do in their own words. An agent could then interpret that request, look at the relevant parts of their calendar, and work out how Reclaim could help. But we needed to address several challenges before introducing agents to the experience. Large language models can interpret the same request in different ways because they generate answers based on patterns in their training data. For example, an open-ended request like “make time for this tomorrow” could lead an agent to find an open block, create a new event, or move something already on the calendar. Each option would affect the user’s schedule differently, and some could affect other people’s calendars, too. That variability made AI agents different from the two paths Reclaim already supported. Although they arrive at decisions differently, all three actors needed to rely on the same scheduling logic. Creating a separate AI-only path would have duplicated functionality and made Reclaim’s behavior harder to keep consistent across interfaces. We needed a system that could connect a model to both the right calendar information and Reclaim capabilities while also controlling how it used them. The result was an agent platform designed to work within Reclaim’s existing architecture. Building the agent platform Our agent platform gives a model relevant calendar details and access to Reclaim’s features while controlling what the model can see and do. The model interprets what the user says and figures out what they want. The agent, meanwhile, manages the larger process by providing Reclaim’s instructions, relevant calendar context, and tools (which let it ask Reclaim to look up information or request a specific action). When a tool returns information, the agent can send it back to the model to inform the next step. This repeated exchange is called the agent loop. As part of this process, Reclaim gives the agent the calendar information and tools relevant to each request, rather than access to everything at once. This helps the agent focus on the immediate task and limits it to the appropriate actions. For a more complex request, the agent can give one specific part to a specialized subagent. Internal checklists and review steps help keep the overall request on track. Ultimately, we opted to build the agent loop, tools, and the system for gathering context ourselves, and we connect directly to model providers instead of relying on a broad agent framework. That’s because a framework we initially explored lagged behind the provider APIs we wanted to use and included more structure than Reclaim needed. Owning these parts lets us design them around Reclaim’s scheduling needs, adopt new provider capabilities more quickly, and work with different model providers without rebuilding the rest of the platform. That leaves us with more code to maintain, though using agents to help with that code offsets some of the additional work. The same tool system supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) in two ways. Inside Reclaim’s agent loop, an MCP client lets the agent use compatible tools from other services. Separately, Reclaim’s MCP server makes selected Reclaim tools available through supported AI clients, including Claude and ChatGPT. Those clients use their own models and agent loops, but can call the same tools used within Reclaim. Our agent platform helped Reclaim work through open-ended requests, but we still needed safeguards around any changes it proposed. Users needed a way to review those changes before they reached their actual calendars. Making calendar changes consistent and reviewable Behind the scenes, Reclaim represents each scheduling capability as a Schedule Action, our internal term for a standard operation like creating or updating an event, changing an RSVP, or finding availability. Whether a request comes from a user, the automated scheduler, or an agent, the same Schedule Action type is used, including the same validation and commit process. That shared path matters because a calendar change can affect more than one event. Moving a meeting might change someone’s availability or cause Reclaim to adjust flexible events elsewhere on a user’s calendar. If each actor used a separate implementation, engineers would have to reproduce those rules and keep every version aligned as Reclaim evolved, which would have become tedious over time. Because all three actors use the same Schedule Action, engineers can change how an operation works in one place rather than updating three separate versions. This helps Reclaim behave consistently across its interfaces. But even when Reclaim handles a change consistently, users still need to see whether its wider effects match what they want to do. That’s why we developed Preview Mode, which gives users a temporary version of their calendar where they can review AI suggestions and changes requested through chat before applying them to their actual calendar. Essentially, they’re able to see how an event or settings change would affect the rest of their schedule before it goes live. They can then confirm that the change behaves as expected and review any effects on shared events before calendar updates are sent to other attendees. To keep Preview Mode fast, we reworked the automated scheduler as a pure function, meaning, in part, that it can calculate a proposed schedule without saving anything to the user’s actual calendar. Reclaim can repeat that calculation whenever the user adjusts the preview. Because busy calendars and meetings with several attendees require a lot of data, Reclaim keeps a readily accessible copy in Redis, a data store designed for fast retrieval. It also updates attendee availability within the preview whenever an event moves, so the next calculation reflects the schedule being proposed. Keeping AI workflows connected Reclaim now has a consistent path from a natural-language request to a reviewed calendar change. The agent platform connects models with relevant calendar information and Reclaim features, Schedule Actions route proposed updates through the product’s scheduling logic, and Preview Mode makes their effects visible before anything reaches the calendar or other attendees. Together, these pieces extend Reclaim with AI while preserving the scheduling experience people already rely on. This work also reinforced what AI needs in order to be useful inside an active workflow. A model needs the surrounding information to understand a request, a controlled way to act on it, and a review step before the result moves forward. In Reclaim, a scheduling goal can move from conversation to a proposed schedule and then to an approved calendar update without requiring the user to translate it into a specific setting or command. The long-term value of this rebuild is the freedom to evolve without fragmenting the product. As AI changes how people ask for help, Reclaim can introduce new capabilities through the same scheduling foundation rather than adding a separate experience each time. For Reclaim, this offers a practical framework for expanding AI-assisted workflows as models improve and people find new ways to manage their time. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Dropbox Tech] Dropbox CTO Ali Dasdan on moving from AI adoption to transformation
summary: As AI becomes a starting point for more kinds of work, its usefulness depends on access to an organization’s trusted knowledge and context, including the files, research, feedback, decisions, and project history that give the work meaning. Dropbox helps people bring that context into the supported AI tools they choose while preserving the permissions and controls they expect, so they can spend less time finding, uploading, and re-explaining what already exists. When AI helps them create something new, Dropbox gives that work a trusted, durable home where it can be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and built on over time. That focus on connected workflows also shapes how we use AI within Dropbox. Access to increasingly capable models can help teams produce more. But turning that output into sustained gains in productivity, quality, and customer impact requires examining workflows from end to end. That includes addressing new bottlenecks as output grows, adapting the platform that supports development, aligning organization-wide incentives, and measuring whether greater speed and volume lead to better outcomes. AI also increases the importance of human judgment. People still need to choose the right problems, give agents the context they need, evaluate the validity of their output, and remain in control of important decisions and actions. Problem solving, communication, and leadership become critical to turning AI-enabled output into real value. Dropbox Chief Technology Officer Ali Dasdan and Senior Director of Engineering Productivity Uma Namasivayam discuss lessons from deploying AI at company scale, how we assess productivity and ROI, how our progress compares with industry peers, and what organizations need to consider as they move from AI adoption to broader transformation. What have you learned in the last year about driving productivity with AI, not just for engineers but across the wider Dropbox organization? Ali: You have to start with the outcome you’re trying to achieve. Giving people AI tools is only the first step. As people use them, your assumptions get tested and new bottlenecks emerge. Maybe you’re coding faster, but now you have too many code reviews. Or you’re generating significantly more code, which puts additional stress on the tools and infrastructure that support development. If you want AI to have a meaningful impact, you have to look at the workflow end to end and keep adapting it until you’re producing the outcome you actually want. There’s no silver bullet. Uma: You have to approach it with a product mindset. Leadership saying, “You need to start using AI tools,” is good, but that alone won’t drive adoption. You also need ground-up awareness through initiatives like boot camps and show-and-tells that involve people more deeply. And you have to align incentives so managers understand what ROI they’re getting from it. How should companies think about measuring AI productivity and ROI? Ali: If I write 10 lines of code and push them to production, it’s almost impossible to prove those 10 lines were responsible for a certain amount of customer satisfaction or revenue improvement. I might produce a million lines a day, but if it’s the wrong product and customers have no interest in it, then it’s not going to work. The real ROI metrics are outcomes like revenue, cost, customer satisfaction, and retention. Then we look at proxy metrics that connect our output to those outcomes. Are we moving faster, producing more code, running more experiments, and pushing more features? Is the site faster and more reliable? There’s no single metric. The framework we use focuses on speed, effectiveness, quality, and impact, with multiple metrics under each. The industry hasn’t found the full solution yet. How does Dropbox’s AI-driven engineering productivity compare with companies operating at a similar level of technical scale and complexity? Ali: If we define peers as top technology companies we hire from and compete with for talent, we’re seeing very similar problems and metrics. We’re around 70% AI-generated code, and Uber recently shared a number around 70%. They see a need for internal agentic coding solutions, and so do we. They have their own tools, and we have Nova, our internal service for running coding agents. Larger companies have allocated more resources to these problems, while we’re super lean. Despite that, I feel like we’re comparable with that peer group across multiple metrics, including how quickly we adopted AI and reached our targets. Compared with the broader industry, it appears we’re ahead. Uma: The industry looks at pull request throughput, or the rate at which teams complete code changes, as one proxy metric for productivity. It’s not ‌perfect, but our throughput ranks in the top 5% in a custom benchmark of companies with similarly large, complex codebases and engineering systems. We also look at whether moving faster affects quality. Our change failure percentage, which measures how often a deployment leads to degraded performance or failure, is in line with industry peers at the 75th percentile. Our token usage is also among the lowest in that peer group, which could indicate that our teams or systems are operating efficiently. Together, these measures give us a fuller picture of how we’re doing against similar companies. As AI usage grows, how do you decide where additional investment is worthwhile? Ali: AI requires money, and when we talk about AI funding, we’re talking about a large portfolio. There are products used by individual functions, capabilities in tools like Zoom and Slack, company-wide deployments like ChatGPT Enterprise, automation tools, and coding models. We’re seeing benefits. People are fixing tech debt, long-running migration projects are getting finished, and we’re delivering most of the roadmap with fewer resources. But organizations still have to decide which ideas to pursue and when to invest more, often before they can draw a direct line to ROI. That requires domain expertise, the right incentives, and a lot of judgment. We’re still working through it along with the rest of the industry. How should companies determine whether their AI spend is creating real value? Ali: At Dropbox, we’re starting to think less about raw token consumption and more about the engineering value those tokens create. With Nova, for example, we can connect agent usage to actual engineering workflows, validation, and outcomes. That gives us a way to evaluate AI spend based on the engineering work those tokens help produce, rather than simply how many tokens we’re consuming. As AI lowers the cost and effort required to produce software, which human skills become more valuable? Ali: If you look fundamentally at what engineers or computer scientists do, it’s that we know how to solve a problem. That’ll never disappear. AI may help me solve bigger problems or solve them faster, but I still need to provide better context, ask the right questions, judge the validity of the answers, know how to iterate, and give a good spec and problem definition. I also need to understand how a solution fits into the broader system and adapt as the tools change. Problem solving, communication, systems thinking, and judgment become even more important because agents depend on people to guide and evaluate their work. Uma: I would give you three things. One is problem solving, which Ali explained really well. The second is judgment. The next phase of AI could make the cost of engineering almost zero, which makes choosing the right problems and evaluating what AI produces extremely important. The third is leadership. Leaders need to understand people, navigate ambiguity as work changes, bring teams together, communicate clearly, build trust, and make sure incentives are aligned. Those skills won’t go away at all. Their value will only grow. As AI models and agents become more widely available, what’ll distinguish the organizations that use them effectively, and what role can Dropbox play? Ali: Models and agents can be incredibly capable, but they don’t automatically know which information an organization trusts, what decisions have already been made, who has access, or what needs to happen next. Without that context, even a strong model can produce generic or incomplete results. Dropbox can connect supported AI experiences to customer-owned content and context, then give the work AI produces a place to be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and continued. People still make consequential decisions, while the work keeps moving without losing the sources, history, and collaborators behind it. A year from now, what do you hope AI-enabled work looks like at Dropbox? Uma: This year, we’ve focused heavily on engineering, and we’re now starting to understand the workflows across product, design, and other non-engineering teams. A year from now, the goal is for people across those teams to be able to come up with ideas, test them with customers, and potentially ship some of those features. If our customer experience team sees an issue, for example, they could use agents to develop a solution and see whether it works for the customer. That’s the vision we’re pursuing internally. If we can prove it works, we could potentially enable external customers to build on Dropbox platforms and use AI with the building blocks we have. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Microsoft Azure] Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
summary: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework. The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards. Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in EnterpriseUnderstanding risk in the deployment contextOpen- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools. The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls. Establishing a common languageManaging these risks consistently also requires a common vocabulary across engineering, security, legal, safety, and business teams. The initial Microsoft and NVIDIA taxonomy organizes risks into five broad categories: Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, and Bias. It is not a policy or deployment checklist, but instead it should be used by enterprises to adapt it to their own systems, use cases, and risk criteria, then connect relevant risks to evaluations, mitigations, and accountable owners. Using evaluations as risk evidenceEvaluations help turn the taxonomy into something enterprises can use. The paper maps evaluations to a selection of risks across the five categories, giving teams a way to start with a risk that matters for their deployment and identify evaluations that can produce relevant evidence about it. Microsoft Foundry helps enterprises assess quality, groundedness, and safety with built-in and custom evaluations and automated red teaming. Its configurable content-safety controls help detect and mitigate harmful inputs and outputs and prompt attacks. Teams should validate control availability for their model and deployment, including preview status, and combine these capabilities with application-specific testing, monitoring, and human oversight. Evaluations still need to be interpreted in the context of a particular deployment and the goal is to make it easier for teams to connect the risks they identify with useful evidence, while building a broader set of evaluation resources that can evolve alongside models, deployment patterns, and emerging risks. Microsoft and NVIDIA plan to use the joint repository to share additional evaluations and point to existing resources that can help enterprises assess specific risks. Accounting for changes in control and responsibilityOpen-weight access gives enterprises greater control over how a model is evaluated, modified, and deployed. Model access and deployment are separate choices: open-weight models can also be used through managed platforms. Responsibility for safeguards depends on the service and deployment configuration; enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service. Those safeguards can operate at different layers, and (depending on the risk) enterprises might use model changes, access controls, input and output filtering, monitoring, or human review. The important step is connecting each identified risk to controls that can effectively address it within the deployed system. Those decisions need to be revisited as models and deployments change. Building on this workRisk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise focuses primarily on the model layer. Future work from Microsoft and NVIDIA is intended to extend this approach across the runtime, harness, and application layers, with additional technical guidance on evaluation and mitigation. We also expect the resources supporting this work to evolve as new models, evaluations, and deployment patterns emerge. The joint repository will provide a place to share additional evaluation resources, including contributions from the broader community. For enterprises deploying open-weight models today, the paper provides guidance they can begin applying to their own use cases. We encourage developers, security practitioners, researchers, and others working in this space to read the paper, explore the evaluations, and contribute evaluations that can help strengthen this shared body of work. title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Server Virtualization Platforms
summary: We’re proud to share that Microsoft has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Server Virtualization Platforms. We believe this recognition comes at an important moment for enterprise infrastructure. The question is no longer simply which hypervisor to run. It is how to create a consistent operating model across cloud, datacenter, edge, and sovereign environments. Microsoft addresses that challenge at two levels: operational consistency through Azure and Azure Arc, and infrastructure consistency through Hyper-V. Read the report From choosing a hypervisor to choosing an operating model For years, the primary virtualization decision was which hypervisor to run. Today, the more consequential decision is how infrastructure will be operated across every environment the business depends on. Virtualization remains a critical foundation, but the value of the platform increasingly depends on how infrastructure is managed, governed, secured, updated, and connected across environments. As infrastructure becomes more distributed, how it is operated becomes as important as where it runs. Microsoft delivers that consistency at two complementary levels: Operational consistency: Azure provides common management, governance, and security across cloud, datacenter, and edge environments. Azure Arc extends those capabilities to distributed infrastructure, giving organizations a unified way to operate diverse environments. Infrastructure consistency: Hyper-V provides a common virtualization foundation across Azure, Azure Local, and Windows Server, helping organizations maintain a consistent infrastructure layer wherever workloads run. Together, these layers help organizations preserve choice without multiplying operational models. Workloads can move, environments can evolve, and new technologies can be adopted without requiring a separate operating model for every environment. Ready for what comes next Operational and infrastructure consistency will become even more important as AI reshapes enterprise IT. Models, agents, applications, and data will increasingly span cloud, datacenter, edge, and sovereign environments. AI alone will not reduce the complexity of distributed infrastructure; in many cases, it will increase the need for common management, governance, security, and infrastructure foundations. Being named a Leader in this Magic Quadrant is an honor for us. More importantly, we believe it reflects a direction many organizations are pursuing: operational consistency across increasingly distributed environments. We remain committed to helping customers combine the flexibility to run workloads where they choose with the consistency required to manage them as one environment.
